turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Nice to meet you, Dr. Smith. Well, I'm here because... we recently put a brighter mirror in our bathroom at home, and ever since then, I just keep noticing the skin around my cheeks and my jawline. 

It looks really uneven to me, or kind of saggy. My husband says he can't really see what I'm talking about, but I see it every time I look, and it's just been bothering me enough that I figured I should come in and talk to someone.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes a persistent preoccupation with perceived uneven or saggy skin on her face that her husband cannot see, which is a perceived defect in physical appearance not observable to others.

turns.doctor_question: When you notice these things in the mirror, do you find yourself spending a significant amount of time checking your reflection or touching your skin to examine it?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, I suppose I do check it a bit more now. Most mornings I end up checking my face from a few different angles in that mirror... and I usually put on a little extra makeup before I leave for the courthouse, just to try and hide it. 

I wouldn't say I spend hours touching my skin, but I definitely look at it more than I used to. I've also noticed that sometimes I catch myself comparing my face to the other women I see at work. And, well, I tend to avoid being in any casual pictures around the office if I’m just not feeling okay about how I look that day.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient confirms engaging in repetitive behaviors related to appearance concerns, such as checking their face from multiple angles, applying extra makeup to camouflage, comparing themselves to others, and avoiding pictures.

turns.doctor_question: How much does this concern about your skin interfere with your daily life or cause you distress when you are unable to cover it up or avoid being seen?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I still get all my work done at the office, so it's not like I can't function. But... the extra time I spend getting ready in the morning, trying to get my makeup right to cover it up, has definitely made me rush into the courthouse a few times lately. 

It's also made me miss the start of my yoga class more than once, which is frustrating. And like I mentioned about the office pictures, I've also skipped being in a few casual photos at my book club and some community events. It just causes me distress to think about how my face might look in them, so I just step out of the frame to avoid worrying about it.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes distress and worry about how their face/skin will look in photos, indicating a preoccupation with their appearance.
symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient describes spending excessive time applying makeup to cover up their skin (camouflaging) and actively avoiding being in photos due to appearance concerns.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever found yourself picking at, scratching, or trying to 'fix' the skin on your face with your fingernails or any tools to try and smooth out the texture?
turns.patient_response: No, I don't really do anything like that. I might touch my face sometimes just to feel if it's as uneven as it looks, but I don't pick at it or scratch it. I definitely don't use any tools on it. I just try to cover it up with makeup like I said.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient denies skin picking but confirms other appearance-related repetitive behaviors, specifically touching their face to check the texture and using makeup to cover it up (excessive camouflaging).

turns.doctor_question: When you look at your skin in the mirror, do you feel that your perception of the unevenness is accurate and that others are just being polite when they say they don't see it, or are you able to acknowledge that your view of your skin might be overly critical?
turns.patient_response: I'm not really sure, to be honest. Um... when I look in the mirror, the unevenness just seems really obvious to me. But I suppose it's possible that I'm being a little too hard on myself. I haven't really thought too much about whether people are just being polite or if they genuinely don't see it... I just know it bothers me when I look at it, but I don't really have a good answer for that.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient confirms being bothered by perceived unevenness in their skin that seems obvious to them when looking in the mirror.

turns.doctor_question: About how many hours a day would you say you spend thinking about the appearance of your cheeks and jawline?
turns.patient_response:
I'm not really sure how to put a number on it, to be honest. I've never really timed it or added it up. 

Um... I definitely think about it a lot when I'm getting ready for work in the morning, and maybe a few times during the day if I go to the restroom or catch my reflection somewhere. But as far as actual hours... I really couldn't say. I just haven't kept track of it like that.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient confirms thinking 'a lot' about the appearance of their cheeks and jawline, indicating a preoccupation with perceived physical flaws.

turns.doctor_question: On a scale from one to ten, with ten being the most intense, how much emotional distress or anxiety would you say this preoccupation with your skin causes you on a typical day?
turns.patient_response: I'd say it's probably around a three or a four. It definitely bothers me, and I feel a bit self-conscious, especially when I'm putting on my makeup or if I think someone is looking too closely. But it's not like I'm having panic attacks over it or anything. It's just a constant annoyance that makes me feel a bit down about how I look.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient confirms being preoccupied with their skin, noting it is a constant annoyance that makes them self-conscious, especially when putting on makeup or if someone looks closely.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever consulted with a dermatologist or a plastic surgeon about your skin or considered any cosmetic procedures to address what you see?
turns.patient_response: No, I haven't. I mean, I've bought different over-the-counter creams and serums that claim to smooth out skin tone and texture, but I've never actually gone to see a dermatologist or a plastic surgeon about it. It hasn't really gotten to the point where I'd consider surgery or anything like that.
